hypotheses.justification: Recover it using h23: J₁ f = J₂ (J₃ f) - J₃ (J₂ f). Both terms belong to F by hF₂ and hF₃, so Submodule.sub_mem applies. Then retain the original proof. This also works when F = ⊥.
Recover it using h31: J₂ f = J₃ (J₁ f) - J₁ (J₃ f). Membership follows from hF₁, hF₃ and Submodule.sub_mem. The original proof then applies, including for F = ⊥.

Recover it using h12: J₃ f = J₁ (J₂ f) - J₂ (J₁ f). Membership follows from hF₁, hF₂ and Submodule.sub_mem. The original proof then applies, including for F = ⊥. Each invariance deletion described here retains the other two invariance hypotheses.

hypotheses.binder: (hskew₁ : ∀ x ∈ F, ∀ y ∈ F, B (J₁ x) y = -B x (J₁ y))
hypotheses.justification: Derive the existing hBsub and hBsub' formulas from hlin and hsymm. Using h23 and the other two skew identities gives B(J₁ x,y) = -B(J₃ x,J₂ y) + B(J₂ x,J₃ y) = B(x,J₃(J₂ y)) - B(x,J₂(J₃ y)) = -B(x,J₁ y). Invariance supplies all required memberships. Insert this recovered hypothesis before continuing the original proof. No nonzero assumption is needed.

hypotheses.binder: (hskew₂ : ∀ x ∈ F, ∀ y ∈ F, B (J₂ x) y = -B x (J₂ y))
hypotheses.justification: Using hBsub and hBsub' (derived from hlin and hsymm), expand h31 and apply hskew₃ and hskew₁ twice: B(J₂ x,y) = B(x,J₁(J₃ y)) - B(x,J₃(J₁ y)) = -B(x,J₂ y). Invariance supplies the memberships, so the original proof can continue unchanged. This includes zero vectors and the trivial module.

hypotheses.binder: (hskew₃ : ∀ x ∈ F, ∀ y ∈ F, B (J₃ x) y = -B x (J₃ y))
hypotheses.justification: Using hBsub and hBsub' (derived from hlin and hsymm), expand h12 and apply hskew₁ and hskew₂ twice: B(J₃ x,y) = B(x,J₂(J₁ y)) - B(x,J₁(J₂ y)) = -B(x,J₃ y). Invariance supplies the memberships. The original proof then applies without any nonzero restriction. Each skew deletion described here retains the other two skew hypotheses.
